surface: Gluon attention cores (m64 target decode, prefill, draft) switch their MFMA dot operands from bf16 to fp16 with fp32 accumulation. gfx908 fp16 MFMA runs at 2x the bf16 rate (CDNA1: 16 K-elements per fp16 instruction vs 8 for bf16; measured 1.51 vs 0.76 TFLOP/s single-CTA, scripts/bench_mfma_rate.py). int8 K/V values and bf16 Q activations are exact in fp16, so the accumulated dots see identical operand values; the softmax-probability cast keeps 11 mantissa bits instead of 8. Instr shape moves to [16,16,16] for fp16. Env levers: VLLM_G128_PREFILL_GLUON_MMA, VLLM_G128_GLUON_MMA, VLLM_G128_DRAFT_GLUON_MMA (fp16 | bf16)
interpretation: Short C6 339.01 tok/s and TTFT 21.1-22.6s are new stack records (prior bests 331.54 and 21.98-22.18). Decode per-stream rates reached 33 tok/s (prior best ~31.4). The staggered-finish overlap metric remains window-sensitive (243-289) while per-stream decode is at record levels. The premise came from user analysis; measured MFMA ratio 1.98x confirms the CDNA1 bf16 half-rate quirk. Note: this fp16 usage is confined to attention-core dots reading an int8 KV cache (exact-value operands); it does not change the bf16 residual stream, W8A8 GEMM dtype, or KV storage.

surface: Graph-safe attention trace design: wrap entry.cudagraph.replay() with stream events, read back post-step
contract: FULL_DECODE_ONLY graphs on (current production), steady C12 2048/256
verdict: Hookpoint is single: CUDAGraphWrapper.__call__ line 361 entry.cudagraph.replay(). Events recorded on the replay stream before/after replay() are captured INTO the graph if recorded inside cuda.graph context, but replay() itself is OUTSIDE capture (normal launch). Implementation: add optional event-pair insertion at capture time (only when VLLM_ATTNTRACE=1), one pair per attention layer (49 events pairs into the graph). On replay, query elapsed times post-step. Cost: 98 event records per step in-graph (~2-3% overhead). This unblocks attention attribution without eager boot.

surface: Concatenated dense GEMM (QKV+gate_up) vs separate at decode M=96
contract: single-GPU microbench, production a8w8 config, M=96 K=2048
candidate: concat N=7168 = 125.5us (saves 104.3us/layer = 5.1ms/step); concat N=6400 = 123.2us (saves 118.7us/layer)
verdict: ACCEPTED microbench. Concatenation is a pure launch-count win (flat GEMM cost across N). 5.1ms/step at TP4 shape (5.1ms of 57.8ms = 8.8%). Implementation needs a production cut: a fused linear that concatenates two checkpoint weights at load (weight concat, one GEMM, split outputs). Checkpoint surgery + serving A/B + acceptance gate are the next slices. The same pattern applies to draft (5 layers).
acceptance: microbench only; serving A/B + quality gate pending

surface: Concat implementation design: QKV+shared-gate_up fuse into one GPTQ linear; MoE gate stays separate (routing semantics)
verdict: Concat candidate is QKV (N=6144: q 4096 + k 1024 + v 1024 at TP4 sharding) + shared gate_up (2x1024=2048) = N=8192 single GEMM. MoE gate (2048->256) CANNOT concat (routing needs its own output; but the concat GEMM could emit it as a column block and split — same launch, output split in-register. TP sharding: all three are ColumnParallel with TP4=4: per-rank N = 1536+512+64 = 2112. GPTQ weights are per-rank shards; concat at load = torch.cat of qweight/scales along N per rank (byte-exact, no retrain). Forward: one gemm_a8w8 call, split outputs by shard sizes. Function-preserving (same math, reassociated order only in K). Serving A/B + acceptance gate next. QKV-only concat (N=6144, no gate) is the smaller alternative if gate sharding fights the concat.

surface: Concat implementation constraints: QKV in attn sublayer, gate_up in MLP sublayer (different forward stages, attention between them)
contract: code trace of vllm/models/flint/model.py layer forward
verdict: The naive QKV+gate_up concat is NOT a bounded edit: FlintDecoderLayer.forward() runs input_norm -> self_attn (QKV, attn, o_proj+collective) -> post_norm -> mlp (gate_up, down). Attention sits BETWEEN qkv and gate_up dataflow (gate_up consumes POST-norm hidden, qkv consumes pre-norm hidden). They cannot share one GEMM without fusing across attention (impossible: attention needs QKV output first). The shippable fusions are WITHIN-stage: QKV itself is already one GEMM (QKVParallelLinear=Merged, N=6144); gate_up is already Merged (N=2048). Per-layer dense GEMMs are already merged where possible. The remaining launch-count is across stages (attn boundary), which no concat fixes. The 5.1ms concat prize assumed co-resident inputs; the dataflow forbids it. The launch problem needs cross-stage fusion (persistent per-layer kernel), which is the kernel build, not weight concat.

The C8 lines are stale history (gates at C8/262k). The LIVE recipe is C12 512k (script C default 12, 512k boot live 2026-11-09, all loop measurements at C12). surface: Draft KV-resident prepare: _precompute_context_kv recomputes projections+RoPE for ALL context tokens every round (fused CK GEMM). KV rows already in cache bind directly via positions+slots.
contract: code read of qwen3_dflash precompute paths + microbench of fused projection at ctx sizes
verdict: The E8 fused projection (one CK GEMM over num_ctx x hidden, L=5 layers fused) is ALREADY one launch per round, not per layer. Hoisting it out of propose saves the GEMM launch (~100us) but the correctness boundary is the per-round slot mapping (draft private rows change per round for rejected tokens). Full hoist needs slot-aware caching (Bolt residency pattern) — a bounded kernel edit in the draft speculator (add a pending-KV-resident flag: if the context rows are unchanged since last round, skip re-projection and reuse cache). Savings are the projection GEMM only (~0.1-0.2ms), not the graph (7.16ms dominates propose). NOT the draft prize; graph GEMM launch-count inside the draft forward remains the larger item.

surface: Draft graph replay (7.16ms) structure: 1 fullgraph replay per round covering 5 draft layers at M=96 (run_fullgraph, not per-layer replays)
contract: code read of DFlash speculator run_fullgraph path
verdict: The draft graph is ONE replay per round (query_cudagraph_manager.run_fullgraph) covering all 5 draft layers + their GEMMs/attn inside the captured graph. Inside-graph launch count is ~25-30 kernels; the 7.16ms is graph GPU time for that subgraph. Per draft layer 1.43ms vs target 0.62ms: draft layers run int8_block KV (dequant per layer) + dense MLP (6144 intermediate) at M=96 with SMALLER graphs (draft capture sizes) and no MoE combine. The per-GEMM cost is the same launch-bound ~110us; draft has ~6 GEMMs/layer = 660us + attn + norms. Target layers have MoE (fused grouped GEMM, 1 launch per gate_up/down) which amortizes better than 6 separate draft GEMMs. The draft prize is draft GEMM fusion within layers (gate_up already fused; QKV+o_proj separate).

surface: Draft MLP fusion audit: gate_up already Merged (Qwen3MLP), QKV merged, o_proj + down separate. Per-layer launches = 4 GEMMs (qkv, o_proj, gate_up, down) + 2 norms + attn.
contract: code read of qwen3_dflash DFlashQwen3DecoderLayer + Qwen3MLP
verdict: Draft per-layer launches: qkv (1 merged GEMM), o_proj (1), gate_up (1 merged, N=2*6144), down (1). 4 GEMMs/layer x 5 = 20 GEMMs + attention x5. At ~110us launch-bound, 20 GEMMs = 2.2ms of the 7.16ms draft graph. Attention + norms + sampling = ~5ms. Draft is already merged where the dataflow allows (same constraint as target: attn between qkv and gate_up). No concat prize inside draft either. Remaining draft lever is the same launch-count problem at M=96: grid occupancy (draft graphs capture at 96 tokens, GEMM grid = 1 x N/128).

surface: Persistent GEMM lower bound: W-stream-only kernel at draft shape (N=6144, W=12MB) = 48us at BLOCK_N=64
contract: single-GPU microbench, W-only stream (no dot, no scales), BLOCK_N sweep
baseline: full GEMM at M=96 N=6144 = 118us (launch-bound flat)
candidate: W-stream floor 48us (BN=64) vs full 118us. Headroom to floor = 70us/GEMM. A persistent kernel that streams W once + adds M streaming + dot must land between 48 and 118 to win; the dot adds M=96 rows of compute so a realistic target is ~70-90us (saves 28-48us/GEMM). At 245 GEMMs/step that is 6.9-11.8ms/step potential. But the kernel is a full rewrite (LDS-resident W tiles, K-loop restructure) — multi-hour, high risk. Floor proven; kernel not built this slice.

surface: Persistent kernel structural verdict: Triton has no LDS exposure; dot-inclusive floor ~56us (W 48 + A 0.6 + MMA 8)
verdict: The persistent-column design cannot be a Triton config change: holding W tiles across M needs LDS, which Triton does not expose. A Triton kernel can only restructure the loop to stream W once per program (already what the tuner does via grid). The 56us floor includes dot; realistic 65-75us. The build is a from-scratch Triton GEMM (not a tuning exercise) — multi-hour with correctness risk equal to the combine bug + serving crash history. This turn: no kernel code. The loop books it as the next multi-turn build only.

surface: Idle 15.6ms vs worker CPU 6.4ms: engine-core round-trip (scheduler->worker->sampler) is on the critical path

The worker CPU (6.4ms) is only part; engine-core scheduling + D2H + output processing make up the rest of the idle. Overlapping the round-trip (async scheduling) is a scheduler feature (VLLM async_scheduling / dual-batch), whose status in this stack was subsumed by the batch-2 PACE regression. No bounded CPU micro-opt closes a scheduler-architecture gap; recorded as the open mechanism.

surface: Standalone CUDA-graph harness replaying 49 layers of prod-shape int8 GEMMs (qkv/o_proj/gate_up/down/router + routed grouped MoE x2 + quant) + lm_head at M=96, to bound the GEMM share of the 38ms target graph.
result: Eager single-call costs are launch/CPU-bound at M=96 (CK GEMM 57us, per-token quant 82us, both dominated by dispatch, while M=1536 reaches 200us = 37 TFLOP/s, i.e. the compute-bound calibration point). The captured harness graph replays in 89ms for the 49-layer GEMM sequence alone, dominated by the two grouped-MoE blocks (~1.2ms/layer) - 2-3x the whole real model graph (30-38ms incl. attention+collectives).
verdict: Harness numbers are not representative: synthetic [E,K,N] int8 expert weights do not reproduce the checkpoint's packed layout/kernel selection, so the grouped GEMM lands on a slow path. A faithful harness needs the real repacked weights (or the vLLM loader), which is not worth the build. Eager micro-benchmarks also cannot stand in for in-graph time (dispatch dominates).

surface: In-graph per-call cost of the five dense GEMMs the decode step issues per layer, M=96 (C12, NS=7 -> 8 rows/stream), prod TP4 shapes, each candidate captured in its own CUDA graph and timed on replay (dispatch excluded).
result: qkv (N=1280,K=2048) 64.8us; o_proj (2048,1024) 41.7us; gate_up (3072,2048) 69.5us; down (2048,1536) 26.2us; lm_head (37536,2048) 228.8us. Sum of the per-layer dense set = 268.5us -> 49 layers ~= 13.2ms/step + lm_head 0.23ms, i.e. 35-45% of the 30-38ms target graph. splitK>0 fails for every shape (RuntimeError: no CK instance), so the CK CSV is not a usable tuning lever here.
verdict: The dense GEMMs are occupancy-starved, not bandwidth-starved: qkv runs 0.5GFLOP in 64.8us = 7.7 TFLOP/s because N=1280 with a 128-wide N tile gives ~10 CTAs for 120 CUs and M=96 cannot fill them; the canonical fix is split-K, which the CK op does not offer for these shapes. Next experiment: in-graph `gemm_a8w8_blockscale` (dense Triton, has split_k configs) at the same five shapes; a 2x win there is ~6ms/step.

surface: Triton dense `gemm_a8w8_blockscale` as a faster replacement for CK a8w8 on the five Flint decode GEMM shapes (M=96), measured in-graph (per-candidate CUDA graph replay).
result: qkv 72.5 vs CK 64.8us; o_proj 39.7 vs 41.6 (tie); gate_up 82.7 vs 70.4; down 52.2 vs 25.6; lm_head 432.9 vs 227.4. Per-token quant alone measures 31-36us in a single-kernel graph, i.e. the single-kernel harness carries ~25-30us of replay overhead, so absolute numbers are inflated but the CK-vs-blockscale comparison is consistent (same overhead both sides).
verdict: Rejected: the Triton blockscale path is slower or equal on every shape, worst on down (2x) and lm_head (1.9x). CK a8w8 stays the dense kernel. With splitK unavailable in CK and blockscale losing, the only remaining lever for the occupancy-limited dense GEMMs is a kernel that partitions K (hipb splitK instances / persistent kernel).

surface: Triton a8w8-blockscale dense GEMM with an explicit config sweep (BLOCK_SIZE_M/N/K, GROUP_SIZE_M, NUM_KSPLIT) at the C12 decode shape M=96, measured in-graph per config (same harness as the CK reference).

Integration needs (a) the tuned 65<M<=128 config branch keyed on N (NUM_KSPLIT=4 for N<=1536, else 1), (b) retaining the GS128 originals for the layers that serve decode M (they are currently freed once _ck_q exists), and (c) a dispatch rule that sends 65<=M<=128 to blockscale and leaves prefill on CK. Quality changes from per-channel to per-128-group scales (closer to the checkpoint), so the acceptance gate applies.

surface: Corrected per-layer cost of the routed-expert grouped blockscale GEMM pair at C12 (M=96) after fixing the per-rank dimensions used by earlier harnesses (moe_intermediate 512/TP4 -> gate_up N=256, down K=128; shared expert 1024/TP4 -> N=512/K=256).
result: grouped pair: 352.6 us/layer (single-call graph), 421.8 us/layer inside a 47-layer graph -> 19.8 ms/step. Earlier harness numbers (1.5 ms/layer, 71 ms/47 layers) were 4x inflated: they used I=512 (unsharded) instead of I_p=128. block_m=8 vs 16 measured 1576 vs 1521 us/layer on the old (4x) shapes, i.e. no win from halving the padded rows.
verdict: The routed-expert GEMM is ~31% of the 63.7ms step and the largest remaining block. Its inefficiency is structural: 256 experts x 16-row tiles for 576 real gate rows pads ~7x, yet halving the tile does not help because the kernel is latency/occupancy bound at these tiny per-expert tiles. Next mechanism is a grouped kernel with smaller block_m plus split-K (write, not select); no available library path covers it.

surface: Config-space sweep of the routed-expert grouped blockscale kernel at C12 (M=96, per-rank dims): block_m 8/16, split_k 2/4 (with and without the fused quant_out epilogue), num_warps 2/4/8, num_stages 2/3.
result: Baseline pair 352.6us (gate_up 209.6, down 154.6). block_m=8 slower (1576 vs 1521 us on the 4x harness). split_k>1 is refused with quant_out (`quant_out requires apply_swiglu with split_k=1`); bypassing it via bf16-out + separate group_quant gave 355.4us (SK=2) and 358.3 (SK=4) - no win. num_warps/stages: gate_up 200-209us, down 141-144us, all within run variance.
verdict: No config-space win: the grouped kernel is latency/occupancy bound at 256 experts x 16-row tiles for 576 real gate rows (~7x padding) and none of the exposed knobs move it. Closed as a tuning target; only a different algorithm (multi-expert tile packing or expert-resident persistent kernel) can improve it. It stays the largest single block at 19.8ms/step.

surface: Coverage/shape audit of the tuned decode-band rule (65<M<=128, bm=32/bn=128/NUM_KSPLIT=4 for N<=1536 else 1) against the linears it actually serves at C12, plus the M=32..48 band (C4-C8) for completeness.
result: shared-expert gate_up (N=512,K=2048): rule picks ks=4 -> 26.8us vs CK 68.3us (2.5x, best of the sweep). M=48: qkv blockscale 23.4 vs CK 32.8 (win) but gate_up 38.4 vs CK 27.8 (loss); M=32: qkv 23.4 vs 24.8 (marginal), gate_up 30.7 vs 26.2 (loss).

surface: Warm-cache TTFT baseline for the FlashStates-style caching work: two-turn agentic pattern (turn 1 = 2048 new tokens; turn 2 = same 2048 + 128 new), single request, greedy.
result: turn1 TTFT 391 ms (2048 new tokens, ~5.2k tok/s prefill). turn2 TTFT 1165 ms (2048 cached + 128 new) - a cache hit is 3x SLOWER than the miss. turn3 (1024-token different prefix + 64 new) 3519 ms.
verdict: Flint's warm-cache path is pathological: reusing a prefix costs more than recomputing it, so the recurrent (mamba) state is being rebuilt over the cached prefix instead of restored. This is exactly the FlashStates target (`vLLM saves recurrent checkpoints only at KV block boundaries and each turn recomputes the end of the previous one`), but here even the block-boundary checkpoint appears unused. Optimizing warm TTFT is now an explicit loop objective.

surface: Mamba prefix caching for Flint (mamba_cache_mode=align) wired through: the deprecated --mamba-cache-mode CLI was dropped on the floor in arg_utils (CacheConfig never received it), so mamba groups never cached and every prefix hit rebuilt the recurrent state. The value now reaches CacheConfig and the flint recipe defaults MAMBA_MODE=align.
contract: Two-turn warm-cache probe (single request, greedy): turn1 2048 new; turn2 same 2048 + 128 new; turn3 different 1024 + 64 new. Plus the standard C12 2048/256 bench at seed 62408.

verdict: Accepted: 4.0x warm-cache TTFT and 7.9x on a partial-prefix hit, decode unchanged/better, acceptance in band. This is the block-boundary checkpoint tier; FlashStates' exact-end frontier checkpoint, cost-aware (GDS) eviction and leaf-last ordering remain as follow-ups.

surface: Fresh-boot confirmation of mamba align-mode caching in the default recipe (no MATCH_UNIT / MAMBA_BLOCK overrides).
result: Two-turn probe: turn1 (2048 new) 411 ms; turn2 (2048 cached + 128 new) 205 ms; turn3 (different 1024-token prefix + 64 new) 548 ms. Pre-fix baselines were 1165 ms and 3519 ms, so 5.7x and 6.4x on this boot (288/444 ms on the earlier boot).
verdict: Caching win reproduces on a clean boot; no config overrides are needed for it. Kept as the recipe default.

surface: After align-mode caching, what dominates a warm-cache TTFT: residual recompute or fixed per-request cost? Probe: seed a 2048-token prefix, then send the same prefix + N new tokens for N=64/128/256.
result: 2048 cached + 64 new -> 204 ms; +128 -> 232 ms; +256 -> 227 ms. Essentially flat in the number of new tokens.
verdict: The residual recompute is already cheap (<30 ms across 64..256 new tokens); a warm TTFT of ~205 ms is dominated by a fixed per-request cost (~120-140 ms above the ~60-80 ms a small prefill step should take). The frontier (exact-end) checkpoint would therefore buy little on this pattern - the next TTFT lever is the fixed overhead (engine wake / first-step latency), not the checkpoint. Priority change recorded; frontier design stays for the agentic case where the residual is large (e.g. tens of thousands of uncached tokens).

surface: Attribution of the ~205 ms warm TTFT: is it prefill work, idle-engine wake-up, or a fixed per-request cost?
result: 64-token prompt: headers 10-19 ms, first token 176-191 ms (first-ever request: headers 187 ms). Same 176-191 ms for a 2048-cached + 64-new turn. Under a concurrent 256-token decode load the probes still read 166-186 ms. So the latency is fixed per request, independent of prompt size, cache state and engine load - it is not prefill compute and not idle wake (the engine blocks on an input queue, so it wakes immediately).
verdict: Warm TTFT floor is ~180 ms from the first-step path itself (admission -> schedule -> forward -> sample -> stream for a new request). That is the next TTFT lever; a step-phase trace of the first step with VLLM_STEPPHASE=1 on a fresh request is the way to split it.

surface: Worker-side phase split of the two-step (prefill+decode) tiny-request workload that exposes the ~180 ms first-token latency. VLLM_STEPPHASE=1 with the new VLLM_STEPPHASE_EVERY=20 cadence, 60 requests of 64 tokens / 2 output tokens.
result: n=120 window: f_tail 11.9-12.2 ms, f_replay 0.36, propose 0.25, s_logits 0.10, s_tail 0.22, s_reject 0.06, everything else <0.1. Total worker time ~12.9 ms/step. Client TTFT for the same requests is ~180 ms across 2 steps, so ~150 ms per request is spent OUTSIDE the worker's step phases (not prefill compute, not sampling).
verdict: The first-token latency is engine/API-side per-request cost, not worker work. Next instrument: VLLM_STEPTRACE on the same tiny-request workload (sched/exec/out per iteration) and, if that is small too, an API-server-side timeline (admission -> engine handoff -> first chunk). Cadence lever VLLM_STEPPHASE_EVERY (default 200) is now available for any future phase window.

surface: Is the ~180-230 ms first-token latency in the streaming (chunk flush) path? 64-token prompts, max_tokens=2, 6 samples each, stream vs no-stream.
result: stream 237 ms mean (192-361); no-stream 230 ms mean (194-398). Identical within noise.
verdict: Rules out the streaming flush / detokenizer chunk path: a non-streaming request waits just as long. The cost is upstream of the response path - request handling between the API server and the first sampled token. Remaining suspects: the draft (DFlash2) per-request context-KV prep, the engine's add_request handoff, or a per-request synchronisation inside the first step that the worker phases do not cover. Next: VLLM_STEPTRACE boot on the same tiny-request workload (sched/exec/out), then an API-server-side first-token timer if exec is small.

surface: Engine-side split of the tiny-request workload (VLLM_STEPTRACE=1, 60 x 64-token prompts, 2 output tokens) to locate the ~180 ms first-token latency.
result: Batch-queue loop: sched 0.10-0.12 ms, exec 42.4-45.5 ms, out 0.04-0.05 ms. The worker's own phase sum for the same workload is ~12.9 ms, so ~30 ms per engine iteration is handoff/wake/IPC overhead. A request needs a prefill iteration plus at least one decode iteration (~90 ms) before the first token, plus admission.
verdict: First-token latency is dominated by per-engine-iteration plumbing (~30 ms over the worker time) multiplied by the 2-3 iterations a fresh request needs, not by compute or by the streaming path. This also explains the ~15-30 ms of pipeline cost inside the C12 step. Next levers: fewer iterations before the first token (e.g. prefill and the first decode in one iteration), or cheaper per-iteration handoff; both are engine-plumbing changes, not kernels.

surface: Separate eager-prefill cost from per-iteration handoff: prefill-only workload (90 distinct 64-token prompts, max_tokens=1) with both VLLM_STEPPHASE and VLLM_STEPTRACE on.
result: Worker phases: f_replay 0.00 (no graph), f_tail 28.7 ms -> the eager prefill step is 28.7 ms vs 12.9 ms for graphed decode steps. Engine: sched 0.10, exec 50.7-52.4 ms, out 0.04. So ~22 ms per iteration is spent in the handoff/serialization between the worker's step and the engine's sampled output, on top of the worker's own 29 ms.
verdict: Both effects are real and now quantified: the eager prefill step (~29 ms at 64 tokens) and a ~22 ms per-iteration handoff. The handoff applies to EVERY iteration, including C12 decode (step 59.3 ms with a ~40 ms worker step), so cutting it toward ~2 ms would take the C12 step to ~40 ms (-33%) and warm TTFT to ~100 ms. This is now the single highest-value remaining target in the loop, and it is engine plumbing rather than kernels.

surface: Post-investigation restore to the plain default recipe (no VLLM_STEPPHASE/STEPTRACE) and a snapshot of served numbers: C12 2048/256 seed 62408 plus the two-turn warm-cache probe.

surface: Arithmetic bound on the routed-expert grouped GEMM: is the 19.8 ms/step block launch-bound (fixable by a persistent kernel) or weight-bandwidth-bound (inherent to small-batch MoE)?
result: Per layer the gate_up tiles cover all 256 experts: 256 x (2048 x 256) int8 = 134 MB of expert weights read per layer, i.e. 6.3 GB per step over 47 layers. At MI100's ~1.2 TB/s that is ~5.3 ms/step of pure weight streaming for the gate_up; measured gate_up is 9.8 ms/step (209.6us x 47) => ~54% of peak HBM. The down GEMM reads 256 x (128 x 2048) = 67 MB/layer (~3.2 GB/step, ~2.6 ms floor, measured 6.6 ms).
verdict: The grouped MoE is bandwidth-bound on expert weights at C12: with only ~2.25 rows per expert there is no reuse to amortise the 6.3 GB/step of weight traffic. A persistent kernel would not change this, and neither would tile packing. The only structural fixes are a larger batch (more tokens per expert, i.e. higher concurrency) or fewer/wider experts (a model change). Close the MoE kernel line; the remaining headroom is ~40% of HBM peak, not 3x.

surface: Correction to FLINT_MOE_BANDWIDTH_BOUND: the bound sets a floor, but the measured kernels sit well above it, so headroom exists.
result: Step weight traffic at C12: routed experts 6.3GB (gate_up) + 3.2GB (down) = 9.5GB; dense linears ~0.33GB; lm_head 2x77MB. Floor at 1.2TB/s ~= 8.2ms/step. Measured: MoE block 19.8ms (gate_up 54% of peak HBM, down ~40%), dense 9ms (far above its 0.27ms floor - the dense GEMMs are launch/latency-bound at M=96, not bandwidth-bound).
verdict: The MoE is bandwidth-bound but only at ~40-54% of peak, so a bandwidth-optimised kernel could plausibly recover 3-4ms/step; that remains a kernel project (persistent/vectorised weight streaming), not config. The dense block is NOT bandwidth-bound - it is the launch/occupancy problem already documented. Previous row's 'close the line' applies only to config tuning.

surface: Routed-expert down grouped GEMM tile: block_n 128 -> 256 with num_stages 2 -> 1 (block_m 16, warps 8). One stage keeps the weight tile at 32 KB so two CTAs are resident per CU and the hardware overlaps their HBM streams.

All other draft shapes (o_proj N=5120 K=1024, down N=5120 K=4352) already sit at their best measured tile. The draft GEMMs are CTA-concurrency bound, not weight-traffic bound: one M tile at bm=128 re-reads the weight 1x instead of 3x and still measures slower on gate_up (333 vs 256 us).
verdict: Accepted. Serving warm C12 2048/256: 652.8/670.0 tok/s, TPOT 57.52/57.55 ms (top of the 619-670 band), acceptance 5.99-6.30 unchanged.

surface: Close the step budget with a direct measurement: VLLM_GRAPH_SYNC=1 times the target graph as wall clock around run_fullgraph + synchronize. CUDA events recorded on the current stream are useless here - the graph replays off that stream, so an event pair reports only the enqueue (3.97 ms against a 37.7 ms step).
result: Target graph = 22.5 ms of GPU per step. Independent kernel sums give 20.5 ms (MoE 13.3 + dense 5.5 + combine 1.3 + lm_head 0.23 + attention 0.2), so ~2 ms is norms/AR/glue inside the graph and the accounting closes. With the draft graph (~7.2 ms) and the sampler (~1 ms) that is ~31 ms of the ~37 ms step; the rest is inter-graph gaps. GPU utilization sampled at 0.1 s during a decode-heavy run: 39% of samples >=90% busy over a window that was ~50% bench wall time.
verdict: Info. The step is GPU-bound; the target graph is the dominant block and 59% of it is the routed MoE, which sits within ~25% of the measured 950 GB/s practical stream ceiling. Kernel work remains the right lever, and the earlier '15.6 ms idle' accounting stays retracted.

surface: Hand-written two-K-loop gate_up tile: stream one 128-column half of the expert at a time (16 KB stages, 2 stages = 32 KB LDS) to get 2 CTAs per CU and a pipelined K-loop simultaneously, then the fused SwiGLU + GS128 epilogue across both halves.
result: Prototype (/tmp/gu_twohalf.py) 199.4-214.4 us vs the stock fused kernel's 185.6 us at the same shapes (M=96 tokens, 576 gathered rows, K=2048, N=256, E=256). Slower at every warps/stages combination tried (4/8 warps x 2/3 stages).
verdict: Closed. The hypothesis was wrong: the down kernel's win came from a wider N tile (128->256), not from occupancy - bn=128/stages=2 was already 32 KB per CTA and already 2 CTAs/CU. gate_up's N is exactly one expert (256) because the fused epilogue quantizes in 128-column output groups, so one whole expert is the minimum CTA work unit and 256 experts over 120 CUs is inherently 2.13 waves. Per wave it already streams at 720 GB/s of the ~950 practical ceiling.

surface: Cache the dequantized int8 base planes of the draft's grouped conv (`_dequant_planes`, built once at load) instead of rebuilding them per call in `_convolve`.
result: Draft graph 6949-6961 us -> 6927-6938 us per step (~20 us, 0.3% of the draft graph). Numerics identical (same int8 codes and fp32 scales).
verdict: Kept: strictly fewer kernels, no behaviour change. But it corrects the hypothesis that the draft's ~4 ms of unattributed graph time is small-kernel overhead - rebuilding those planes 20x/step only cost 20 us.
acceptance: 5.71-6.49 mean acceptance length across the three measurement runs (band 5.0-6.3, gate floor 3.95); the draft graph is unchanged numerically.

surface: Ablation to attribute the draft graph: VLLM_DRAFT_ABLATE=attn replaces the draft layer's self_attn with zeros (numerics deliberately broken) so the existing [dsub] draft_graph timer, which is measured outside the graph and works, splits attention from the rest.
result: Draft graph 6927-6961 us -> 2596-2607 us. The draft's 5 attention layers cost 4.33 ms/step (0.87 ms per layer); the rest of the draft graph is 2.60 ms (four big GEMMs 1.9, conv ~0.3, kernel_projection GEMMs, norms). Acceptance collapsed to 1.00, confirming the ablation took effect. draft_max_seq_len is correctly bounded (min(seq_len+8, max_model_len)), so the KV walk is not padded.
verdict: Info: this is the largest remaining named item in the step. The draft attention runs at ~58x its bytes bound and ~300x its compute bound at M=96 over 12 sequences x 2300 keys with 2 kv heads per rank, and is 8.7x the target's per-layer attention at a nearly identical shape - so it is pathological, not merely small. Next: microbench the draft attention call at this shape and find why it diverges from the target path.
acceptance: n/a (diagnostic; service reverted to the production path and re-validated at 648 tok/s)

surface: Diagnostic A/B of the KV dtype to test whether the per-128 block dequant is the attention cost: KV_DTYPE=int8_per_token_head (no block scales) vs the recipe's int8_block_g128, at C12 2048 input.
result: period 41.96 ms with int8_per_token_head vs 38.89 with int8_block_g128; acceptance 4.27 vs ~5.9. Dropping the block scales is slower AND worse quality.
verdict: Closed: the block dequant is not the attention cost. With the earlier rejects (BLOCK_M query-split, AITER_UA_FORCE_3D) and the finding that the 3D path already KV-segments 8-way, every config-level lever on attention is exhausted; the residual ~15 ms/step is the kernel's intrinsic per-tile efficiency. Also fixed a real latent bug in our aiter fork: select_2d_config used os.environ with no `import os`, so any KV dtype routing to the 2D path crashed at boot.
acceptance: Recipe re-validated on int8_block_g128 after the run: 583 tok/s, acceptance 5.26.

surface: Tool calling on the flint recipe: --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser glm47 (TOOLPARSER lever)
why: Flint's chat template declares <tool_call>{name}<arg_key>k</arg_key><arg_value>v</arg_value></tool_call> plus <|observation|><tool_response>, which is GLM-4.7's format; the shipped glm47 parser matches it unchanged, so no new parser was needed.
perf: not measured: parser cost applies only to requests carrying tools and is per-token lexing; the standard steady bench sends no tools. No perf claim.
verdict: ADOPTED. The recipe default boots with tool calling on; TOOLPARSER="" reverts to a no-tool boot.

surface: Mandatory performance procedure: three-phase cycle + workload matrix + metric contract
phases: 0 numeric contract freeze; classify changes numerics-preserving vs numerics-changing (the latter decided before PTQR or they force a re-PTQR)
1 inference tuning with the draft running and every draft force-rejected at the sampler, keeping M = C x (NS+1); never via skip_drafts, which collapses M to C
2 PTQR with sampled acceptance gates (temperature 1.0, per-position, serving NS, two context bands) and draft-vs-target distribution metrics
3 NS and draft KV/quant tuning with real acceptance; total request time at W1/W3
workloads: W1 agent-steady (shared warm prefix, tools, recipe sampling), W2 agent-cold (distinct prompts), W3 long-turn, W4 mixed 6+6, W5 witness C1 (pathology only, never a target)
metrics: usage/Prometheus token counts; per-stream and fully-overlapped aggregate; acceptance with per-position vector; tokens/step and ms/step always reported with throughput; TTFT cold/warm; prefill tok/s with chunk shapes; p95 ITL; total request time primary
protocol: one warm-up + >=3 repeats with spread; pinned cache state; paired/interleaved on one boot for kernels; effect must exceed pooled spread or win >=4/5 pairs; boot fingerprint recorded
gates: reject if W1 median acceptance drops >0.10; NS/draft decisions only at served sampling; four-arm attribution (draft int8/bf16 x KV int8/bf16) at temp 1.0
verdict: ADOPTED. docs/recipes/optimization_procedure.md is authoritative; it supersedes earlier performance guidance and all pre-2026-11-10 throughput numbers.

attribution: At C12/18k (~155ms): attention ~54ms (context slope), MoE ~17ms, dense ~5.6ms, draft ~3.8ms, sampler ~1ms -> ~80ms accounted; the remaining ~55-75ms scales with concurrency (C1 base 40.6ms vs C12 base 101ms at 2.4k) and is NOT explained by attention (6ms), MoE, dense or draft micro-benchmarks.

surface: Differential boot: KV dtype bf16 (diagnostic only, banned for production) vs int8_block_g128, phase-1 isolation (FORCE_REJECT=1), C12 W1
result: bf16 KV is 1.48x faster at 2.4k and 1.77x at 18k. The int8 KV path costs +33 ms (2.4k) to +67 ms (18k) per step, which is the context-scaled block that the kernel micro-benchmarks did not predict.
why_it_matters: KV bandwidth is not the limit (int8 halves bytes and is still slower); the cost is the packed block-g128 dequant path in the unified attention kernel. Attention FLOPs at 18k are ~0.5-3 ms, so the kernel is running at a few percent of peak.
verdict: PRIME PHASE-1 LEVER: optimize the int8 KV dequant (or evaluate int8_per_token_head) rather than any weight-side kernel. bf16 KV itself stays banned per the int8-first directive.

surface: Acceptance vs prompt shape, same recipe and KV dtype (block_g128), served sampling
result: Acceptance is strongly corpus-dependent: docs prose ~2.7, agent/tool traffic ~1.0-2.4. The engine's own metrics agree with the harness when the same window is used.
verdict: W1 must be agent-shaped (system/tool prefix + short user turn), not a prose prefix; scripts/bench_cycle.py now sends the shared prefix as the system message and a short unique user turn. Any acceptance claim must name the corpus.

surface: Run-to-run variance of the W1 harness on one boot, identical prompts and config
verdict: Two identical consecutive runs differ by 2.2x. Single-run A/Bs are invalid; the procedure's >=3 reps with median+spread is mandatory, and paired/interleaved arms are required for sub-20% effects. Investigate the first-run penalty (cache warmth / clock ramp) before trusting any single boot.

surface: int8_per_token_head KV vs int8_block_g128 KV, forced-rejection step time (the acceptance arm was equal: 2.70 vs 2.75)

surface: Switch the Flint recipe KV layout from int8_block_g128 to int8_per_token_head (target and draft), measured under the procedure (agent-shaped W1, served sampling, 3 reps/arm)
why: Both layouts use the same int8 quantization math (one fp16 scale per token-head; group = head_dim in kv_block_quant_fake), so this is a cache layout change, not a precision change. The block_g128 packed writer path was the slower layout on this kernel.
result: +21.5% per-stream at 2.4k and +57% at 18k, with equal-or-better acceptance (engine metrics confirm 3.16-3.55 at 18k).
verdict: ADOPTED in scripts/serve_recipe_flint.sh (default KV_DTYPE=int8_per_token_head; rollback KV_DTYPE=int8_block_g128). Quality battery and KLD remain part of the phase-2 PTQR gate; the earlier 'per_token_head slower and worse quality' note is contradicted for speed and predates the launcher import-os fix.

surface: PTQR trainer max sequence length on 4x32 GB (teacher-streamed, TP4, grad_checkpoint, kd_cache=1)

legs.seq_len_16384: CUDA OOM: tried to allocate 8.00 GiB with 7.46 GiB free (23.49 GiB already allocated per rank)
legs.cause: full-vocab teacher logits: T x 248320 x 2 B. 16k -> 8.1 GiB; 4k -> 2.0 GiB (the rung-1 s40 run that succeeded). Student head and loss are already chunked (one_batch, logits_chunk); the KD-cache warm runs the teacher head unchunked.

The 512k-scope corpus legs exist (tier 5) but are only ever sampled in seq_len windows.

StreamedFlintTeacher._head_chunked: the KD-cache sweep applied the full-vocab head to the whole sequence; now chunked (1024 rows) so device logits stay bounded.
one_batch keeps the cached teacher logits in fp16 and casts per loss chunk; the previous whole-tensor .float() doubled memory (16.3 GiB at 16k).

surface: Trainer checkpoint saves + the truncated-shard mystery
findings: a full master shard is ~20.2 GB per rank (39.8B bf16 / TP4), not 5.5 GB: every existing ptqr_target_step*_rank*.pt is a ~27% partial write
the partials are saves killed mid-file by the run timeout; the save itself takes ~6-8 min for the 4-rank set (76 GB)
the post-eval 'stall' seen twice was the step-0 save running, not a hang

surface: Why a fresh PTQR student starts at CE 11.0 / KLD 9.2 while rung 1 started at loss 3.0 / KLD 0.077
established: the step-0 gap is not dither: tau=0 (temp_start=temp_end=0) still gives ce 11.04 / kd 9.12 / eval KLD 9.19

the rank shards are geometrically CORRECT: shard q_proj (1280 rows) equals bf16 q_proj[:1024] + k_proj[:128] + v_proj[:128] exactly (maxdiff 0.0); embed and gate_proj match contiguous row slices exactly
the streamed teacher's cached logits are sane (teacher_nll 3.26 on the same val batches), so _head_chunked is fine
the student is built on a meta skeleton, sharded, then to_empty(device) -> UNINITIALIZED memory, then filled by load_flint_rank_shard from the shard keys only
prime_hypothesis: the source shard does not cover every student tensor (fused-qkv and expert remaps are handled, but some trainer-side tensors stay uninitialized), so a subset of weights is garbage at step 0. The 9564 shard tensors vs the trainer's richer key set is the place to diff.
next: bisect the build on one GPU with the trainer's exact steps: (a) bf16 student after load, before the PTQR swap - CE should be ~2.8; (b) after replace_linears_with_ptqr; (c) after fake_quant_embedding_. Whichever step first shows CE ~11 is the bug, and diffing the shard keys against the student state_dict names gives the missing set.

surface: Why the fresh PTQR student disagrees with the streamed teacher despite identical weights
evidence: every compared weight is bit-identical between the loaded rank-0 student and StreamedFlintTeacher._stage_layer: qkv/o/sink (L0), router/shared/experts x3 (L2), maxdiff 0.0 on all
with dist disabled (no TP reduce on either side) the module forward and _apply_layer disagree on layer 0 with identical inputs and weights: maxdiff 0.1235, meandiff 0.0206, corr 0.9661
PTQR_DEBUG_IDENTITY=1 (quantization bypassed) still gives top1 0.031 / corr 0.217 / sorted_corr 0.561 versus the cached teacher logits
conclusion: the student (module path) and the KD teacher (_apply_layer) are NOT the same function. The trainer distills the student toward _apply_layer's logits, so a structurally diverging teacher explains the fresh-init CE 11 / KLD 9.2 without any weight or save problem.
open: which path is correct. The serving stack is the authority: compare greedy continuations/logits from the deployed checkpoint (and ideally the bf16 model) on the same prompts against _apply_layer's cached logits. If _apply_layer is wrong, the whole PTQR KD program distills toward bad targets.
next: L0 sub-output bisect (attention vs MLP), then a serving-vs-teacher continuation check

surface: Fresh PTQR student CE 11.0 / KLD 9.2 - root cause and fix
root_cause: the shared attention-mask helper I added for long-context training tested a bare `if window:`. Full-attention layers carry window = -1 (the no-window sentinel), which is truthy, so their masks were ANDed with (qi - ki < -1) and became all-False; softmax over an all-masked row yields zeros, so every full-attention layer produced zero attention.
evidence: _allowed_mask(8, -1, cpu) returned an all-False mask; with per-module masks (before the change) full-attention rows were causal
after the fix, student module forward vs StreamedFlintTeacher._apply_layer is bit-identical at L0 (dense) and L2 (MoE): maxdiff 0.0, corr 1.0
fresh student step 0 is now loss 3.4302 / ce 3.2897 / kd 0.0703, eval KLD 0.091108 (was 29.29 / 11.04 / 9.12 / KLD 9.19); debug logits top1 0.781, corr 0.9931, sorted 0.9969
verdict: FIXED. The weight, shard, save and teacher paths were all sound; the failure was this regression. Phase-2 rungs can proceed from the bf16 base (no master checkpoint needed).

verdict: No repeatable throughput gain. Fully overlapped C12 decode stayed flat and mixed rates were more variable. Both five-run batches on the new stack include slow cold admissions. Three of three serial greedy hashes changed. No attribution to a specific dependency.
provenance: The host toolkit stayed at HIP 7.14.60850. AMD gfx908 wheels supplied the new Python runtime. The native vLLM extensions and the AITER Torch-bound GEMM were rebuilt.

workload: W4; six primed 2048-token real prompts, six cold prompts of 2048 tokens at +2s; 256 output tokens per request; aggregate prefill and all-stream decode measured over the same cold admission window.
hardware: 4x MI100 XGMI, each capped at 105 W. Native Flint TP4/C12/NS7, budget 2048. Scheduler chooses the token count per iteration.
cache: The first six prompts share a primed prefix namespace. A fresh namespace is used for the injected six every run. The original 2.13 server retained its on-disk and process Triton caches across the trace and later control.

profile.stack: Live TP worker samples in Triton AMD machine-code generation below the fused SiLU projection. All four worker profiles contained compiler frames.

isolated_fix.bitwise: Identical old vs new INT8 codes, FP32 scales and dequantized output at every row count. After warm-up no new compiled binaries for later odd lengths in the same tile class.
isolated_fix.silu_probe: Single MI100 at 105 W; gated N1024 K2048 and ungated N640 K1536; separate empty Triton cache for the comparison; use one decode and one prefill length to prime tile classes for each width. Alternate arm order for eight unseen lengths, synchronized first-call wall time including JIT. Medians over 16 paired shapes. Outputs and scales bit-identical.

verdict: Four kernels over-specialized on scheduled row counts or a derived grid. Their fixed binaries now serve variable rows. Whole-server runs above are controls on original workers; no patched-server throughput inference from the isolated timings.

surface: Flint serving quality and optional reasoning extraction
contract: Existing native workers; four gfx908 at 105 W, TP4/C12, INT8 block-G128 KV on target and draft, DFlash NS7; PyTorch 2.13.0+rocm7.14.0.

validation.short_chat: 48 passed, 4 failed at the 1,536-token limit; four separate retries finished at 4,096. All 52 returned visible text and finite logprobs. Omit enable_thinking=false on the original workers; reasoning budget 384.
validation.tools: 10/10 streaming and non-streaming tool selection and round-trip checks.
validation.retrieval: 3/3 serial numbers on both passes at 42,082 input tokens.
validation.long_documents: 4/8 completed with the original 4,096-token cap. 6/8 finished with the same cap and 1,024 tokens for reasoning; some visible planning and duplication. Risk analysis finished on a separate 16,384-token retry. The one-request API inventory still truncated at 16,384. Chunk extraction and a source-span follow-up recovered all 138 distinct declaration names.
validation.parser: Old parser exposed explicit reasoning in 52/52 transcripts with enable_thinking=false. Fixed parser recovered 26 finals and correctly isolated 26 unfinished reasoning blocks. All transcripts replayed through the composed serving stream parser in one- and seven-token batches.

limitations: Parser fix verified by offline replay and regression tests. Workers were kept running. Unrestricted exhaustive single-request inventory remains open. The source-span check scores declarations only.

contract: 4 MI100 XGMI, board caps 105 W each, TP4/C8, NS7, K128/R64. All hardware component trials use per-rank production dimensions.
storage: GPU-resident weights, bcache Engram, independent same-GPU snapshots for operator replays

rates: Aggregate decode measured in the fully concurrent interval. Cold prefill divides all prompt tokens by the interval from the earliest send to the last request’s first token.
decisions: Widening each causal value tile to 256 channels and sharing page addresses increased aggregate cold prefill by 5.3% in paired runs.

On XGMI the recipe divides long IndexPool searches by query row and gathers the selected IDs. The 512-token full-model append took 2.8% less time at 65,536 tokens, 7.8% less time at 131,072 tokens. Greedy output also matched on appends of 513, 777 and 1,023 tokens.
The selected XGMI collective configuration increased aggregate cold prefill by 13.4% across eight interleaved comparisons. It raises the custom all-reduce message limit from 8 to 64 MiB.
Combining routed and shared expert reductions removed 41 calls from the captured target graph. The serving comparison retained separate reductions.

Layer-specific expert fusion was tested across all 41 routed layers and on two independent verification inputs. 3 layers passed the operator gate. The end-to-end gate retained the existing verify schedule.

scope: TP-local complete GEMM/operator timings at four-card simultaneous load; all four MI100s at 105 W
control: The existing tuned GS128 GEMM and deferred-scaling matrix-only kernel

numerics.affine: original NeUQI scale/zero; A8 signed high, biased signed low, and 8 times sum of centered W4 weights

activation_preparation: INT8 low signed nibble after xor 8, high signed nibble; restore 8 * sum of signed weights. Last tuning pass includes the GPU activation packing kernel in the timed interval. Weights are already packed.
weight_sum_options: computed with native INT4 DOT8 per K group or cached for each channel and group
labels: C and D add vector rows; D interleaves drain from previous K group. Data, output, and tensor sizes are unchanged. Fences restrict compiler reordering; only disassembly establishes instruction placement.
schedule_clock: HIP events around graph replay, shuffled paired arm order, per-card median then median across four cards; elapsed microseconds

serving_W2.dispatch: All measured hybrid runs reused a compiled FlyDSL launcher for each kernel. Graph-replay operator timings exclude host JIT overhead.

change: Engine core pinned to 12 physical cores (24 logical: 28-39,76-87) instead of 8 (28-35,76-83); the recipe sizes it with mi100_cpu_map.py --parent 12 8. CPU affinity only: same kernels, same batches, bit-identical outputs.
why: The live worker waits ~1.3 ms every step for the engine's next RPC (same at 2k and 40k): the engine core's per-step chain (update_from_output 0.65 ms + schedule 2.85 ms + IPC) runs after the previous output and lands ~1.3 ms after the worker finishes the draft; the engine process runs ~290 threads (HIP/omp pools, ZMQ I/O) on 8 logical CPUs, so the chain is slower than the same code in-process. The exposed cost is larger than the wait itself: the worker reaches the graph replay launch ~2 ms late, and that launch costs ~2 ms of CPU with the side-stream overlaps, so the GPU idles ~2 ms/step in the live service versus 0.4 ms in-process.

why: The live decode step leaves the GPU idle only 0.45 ms after the draft; the engine/worker CPU chain is hidden behind the sampler tail and draft, so a GPU-side saving shows up only if the CPU chain is not the new limit. The tiles shorten the sampler tail; the early-out shortens the chain.

Tiles: bit-identity at M=96 recorded in INKLING2MINI_C12_WIDE_HEAD_TILES_20261124.
verdict: Small, real decode-step gain (0.2-0.9 ms per step depending on the pair; the two later controls were also slower overall, so part of that gap is boot-to-boot drift). Serving tok/s for the three workloads is pending a gate measurement.

change: Inkling-2-Mini served from docker/mi100 (ROCm 10.2, torch 2.15) with MI100_RECIPE=inkling2mini. Image fixes: the build context now ships scripts/serve_recipe_inkling2mini.sh, mi100_host_kv.py and mi100-recipe-lifecycle.sh (the launcher and the helpers it needs were missing from the whitelist); AITER_REV points at the commit carrying the routed-expert and tabulated-SwiGLU kernels the recipe loads; the dispatcher prefers the PTQR-retrained checkpoint and bounds RCCL staging for inkling2mini in the container (NCCL_BUFFSIZE=1048576, NCCL_MAX_NCHANNELS=4); the launcher passes the four-way expert split only on 4 ranks; the dispatcher rejects 3 cards.
design: docker compose (project mi100, port 8120), retrained target and draft under /models, production CPU map on 4 cards. Each configuration: container up until /v1/health 200, then one chat request (128-token budget). First boot per tensor-parallel size compiles AITER kernels (cold JIT cache).

results.3_cards: rejected up front: 24 heads and 8 KV heads cannot be sharded over TP=3 (all workers hit the head-divisibility assertion) and the launcher has no pipeline mode

findings: Both 4-card configs first failed the workers' startup memory check (27.5-27.8 of 31.98 GiB free vs 0.92 required): RCCL's default staging in the ROCm 10.2 container held about 4 GiB per card; the hy4 case already bounded it, inkling2mini did not.

2 cards first failed because the four-way expert split [36,36,20,36] was passed unconditionally; 2 cards now use the model's even split (a different summation order from the retrained 4-rank layout; functional, not the measured configuration).
Diagnostic run on 4 cards: KV cache 2,310,352 tokens (host service 2,299,823), /v1/models max_model_len 1048576, an image request answered 'Blue'.
scope: Functional validation only: no throughput was measured in the container. The 4-card passes were on the build before the 2-card and 3-card fixes; those edits do not touch the 4-card path.

change: Inkling system service uses VLLM_GFX908_MIXED_PREFILL_INTERVAL=4. The existing shared 1024-token mixed budget and 4096-token bulk budget remain active. Kernel and model settings are identical across arms.
incident: From 18:00 UTC Nov 25 to power loss, all 320 ten-second samples with >=6 requests running and <=60 aggregate generation tokens/s included mixed prefill with a 1024-token prompt chunk. At 09:14:43 UTC, 37.8 generation tokens/s with 9 requests running and mean acceptance 3.94; decode-only rounds followed the final prefill chunk.

contract_details.pair: PTQR W4A8 Vision r2 + DSpark PTQR W8A8 r2

design.repeats: One warmup, then three measured per arm; uncontended sets listed. Numbers in triplets are median, minimum and maximum across measured repeats. Per-position vectors are elementwise medians.
design.W4: 8 established streams with disjoint cold 2048-token real-code prompts and 768-token budgets. After every stream emits, inject 1 request with a GPU-warmed 196608-token prefix and 24576-token fresh suffix, 1 output token. Rotate the first 2048 suffix tokens each repeat. All eight streams overlap the entire injection. Measure exact streamed token IDs in the send-to-first-token window. Input throughput counts logical suffix tokens. Mixed-step time uses per-stream speculative-round counter deltas bracketing the injection.
design.W4_shapes: mixed M=1088 (1024 prompt + 8 x 8 verify), final partial chunk, decode-only M=64 at eight streams
design.W1: 12 concurrent chat+tools streams; explicitly warm shared ~16k real-code prefix; 256 sampled output tokens; M=96 at full overlap.
design.ttft: W1 warm; W4 new suffix behind warmed prefix. Fully cold 24k-suffix pilot used the initial control only.
design.clock_policy: Existing thermal controller throughout. During the initial control the cap fell from 123 to 98 W. Compare the candidate to the return control as well.

baseline.note: Original control at a higher power cap. Customer traffic overlapped repeat 3. The isolated return control supplies the three-repeat reference.

quality: At idle all four 32-token greedy sequences matched between the repeat candidate and the return control. Initial control canaries under customer load differed on three prompts. The micro gate passed and the GPU battery passed 4/4.
limits: The wider cold and long-output matrix encountered customer traffic on the original control and was discontinued. The verdict is scoped to incident mitigation on the host unit; no general launcher or kernel change. 500 tok/s is not established for concurrent long prefill.
verdict: Deploy interval 4 for this service. At similar controller caps the eight incumbent streams produced 103.7 aggregate tok/s during the injected prefill versus 39.5 in the return control. The median incumbent stream gained from 4.84 to 12.23 tok/s. Injected TTFT went from 20.53 to 26.82 s. W1 request p50 was 8.18 versus 8.29 s and full-overlap decode was 409 versus 422 tok/s. Mixed-window improvement exceeded repeat spread.
